images.caption: Figure 1:Entropy spikes in denoising dynamics. (a) A representative example illustrating the correlation between entropy spikes and hallucinations. Tokens committed at steps with an entropy spike closely correspond to hallucinated content in the response. (b) Mean mask entropy decreases steadily across denoising, while a few steps show sharp rises that break the local trend, which we refer to as entropy spikes. (c) A step is flagged as an entropy spike when its stepwise entropy change exceeds theμ+σ\mu+\sigmabound from the calibration window.

Figure 2:Entropy spikes characterization across decoding steps. (a) Token-level scatter of stepwise entropy change on LLaDA-V (top) and Dream-VL (bottom). Roughly 80% of hallucinated tokens fall in the area aboveμ+σ\mu+\sigma. (b) Distribution of entropy spikes across denoising steps on LLaDA-V (top) and Dream-VL (bottom). On both models, entropy spikes mostly occur in the early-to-middle decoding stage, when few tokens have been committed and the available context is still limited. (c) Effect of random remasking on performance using LLaDA-V. Top: replacing low-confidence remasking with random remasking at 10% of randomly selected steps causes a substantial drop on three datasets. Bottom: applying the same random remasking only at entropy spike steps yields negligible change. At entropy spike steps, confidence signals may become less discriminative, making discrete commitment decisions less reliably grounded in the current contextual information.

Figure 3:Example visualization of StepRefine. At an entropy spike step, StepRefine reshapes the predicted distribution at masked positions, shifting the prediction toward a more context-consistent candidate, which is then committed. More qualitative examples are provided in AppendixC.
